positions.text: Silva, Aparício, and Silva provide independent evidence for the narrower credit-propagation mechanism in Kaal's claim. Their author-ranking study distinguishes paper-level networks, which diffuse scientific credit to cited papers and then derive author credit from those papers, from author-level networks, which diffuse credit directly to cited authors. PageRank further weights a citation from an important author more heavily and updates an author's score from incoming citation links. This qualifies Kaal's proposition that standing can propagate through a graph rather than accrue only at the original contribution. The study concerns human scholarly impact, treats citations as credit-bearing edges without Kaal's institutional-validation condition, and does not establish autonomous agents, domain-specific REP, or the broader governance substrate.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: Traditional bibliometrics have, however, the drawback of assigning impact to direct citations only, thus ignoring indirect citations. For example, if A cites B, and B cites C, traditional bibliometrics give no additional credit to C from A's indirect citation.
This idea extends naturally to citation networks, i.e., it is good to be cited by any author but is better to be cited by important authors.
Graph-based metrics, on the other hand, spread the credit to previous works that paved the way
paper-level ranking uses the papers' citation network to diffuse scientific credit to cited papers, and then authors credit is derived from the credit of their papers
author-level ranking uses the authors' citation network to diffuse scientific credit to cited authors, thus the authors' credit is directly obtained
Score term (ST) updates the score of a node Ai, according to the score of his in-links (i.e., nodes citing Ai).
